Responses were collected from 209 contractors across 37 U.S. states; Washington, D.C.; Guam; and the Marshall Islands, covering both residential and commercial buildings. Consistent with findings from other studies on labor market experiences, many contractors expressed a desire to grow their business but are struggling to find and hire qualified workers. This challenge is largely attributed to gaps in technical and soft skills. The issue of skill gaps also affects the existing workforce, as many contractors reported that a significant portion of their current staff are not well trained. To support workforce programs that are working to address these industry needs, this study offers valuable insights into contractors’ training decisions. When looking at training versus hiring, upskilling existing staff is preferred when skill gaps are small—for example, when new technologies, codes, or programs require it, which is often how energy efficiency work is addressed. Hiring, on the other hand, is often preferred when time is limited, the skill gap is too large to close through training, or a new hire brings a fresh perspective or unique experience. Although delivering high-quality work is a primary concern and skilled workers are a priority, contractors often hesitate to invest in training due to the costs of training and fears that employees may leave shortly after completing training. The demands of busy work schedules and the potential loss of income while employees are training exacerbate these concerns, underscoring the need for programs to offer short, flexible training options for employees during off-peak seasons, as well as subsidies to not only help offset training costs, but also to compensate companies for workers’ time spent taking the training. The survey results also emphasize the importance of hands-on, on-the-job training for both new trainees and current employees seeking upskilling. Many contractors indicated that, if offered training subsidies for their workers, their top preference would be to use funds to conduct training in-house and on the job, with other in-person courses being the second most preferred. Furthermore, contractors place significant value on demonstrated experience and competence when hiring new workers, often finding candidates through recommendations and apprenticeship or internship programs.
